hook.line: Messages are flying to the coast, and half of them are "tell him to call me". Passing on a request is different from passing on news, and the verb ending is what shows it.
hook.en: Vale says for you to call her. (to a friend)

examples.en: Vale says for you to call her. (to a friend)

examples.es: Mi mamá me pide que vaya el domingo.
examples.en: My mom is asking me to go on Sunday.
Tell him to wait. (to a friend)

examples.en: Hernando wants you to come to the café. (to a friend)

examples.en: Tell Tomás to call him. (to a stranger or someone older)

rule:
In English a request is "tell her *to call*", with *to* and the plain verb. In Spanish the two halves are joined by *que*, and the second verb changes its ending.

*Decir que* or *pedir que*, then a verb with the "opposite" ending:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *llame*, *espere*, *hable*
*-er/-ir* verbs take *-a*: *vaya*, *venga*, *escriba*

For *you* (to a friend) add *-s*: *llames*, *vengas*.

The person asked is the one who does it, so there is no "to": *Dile que espere* = "tell him to wait".
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive: the mood Spanish uses when one person wants another to do something.

options: Vale says she calls you.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose the right form and type the whole sentence (Vale says for you to call her. To a friend): Vale dice que la ___. (llamas / llames)
yourTurn.why: A request to a friend ends in *-es* for an *-ar* verb: *llames*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose the right form and type the whole sentence (Tell him to wait. To a friend): Dile que ___. (espera / espere)
yourTurn.why: A request uses the "opposite" ending, so *espere*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: My mom asks me to go on Sunday.
yourTurn.answer: Mi mamá me pide que vaya el domingo.
yourTurn.why: *Pedir que* plus *vaya*, the request ending of *ir*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a friend): I'm asking you to write to me today.
yourTurn.answer: Te pido que me escribas hoy.
yourTurn.why: *Te* is your friend, and *escribas* is the request ending for *you*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a stranger): Tell Tomás to call him.
yourTurn.answer: Dígale a Tomás que lo llame.
yourTurn.why: To a stranger the command is *dígale*, and the request verb is *llame*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Hernando wants you to come to the café. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: Hernando quiere que vengas al café.
yourTurn.why: *Querer que* also takes the request ending: *vengas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about *me*: Vale dice que la llames. (Vale says for me to call her)
accept: Vale dice que yo la llame.
yourTurn.why: For *I* the *-ar* request ending is plain *-e*: *llame*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After a request, the second verb takes the "opposite" ending: *espere*.
English uses *to call*, but Spanish joins with *que* and a changed verb.

pitfalls.wrong: Mi mamá me pide que voy.
pitfalls.right: Mi mamá me pide que vaya.
pitfalls.why: *Ir* is irregular in a request: *vaya*, not *voy*.
After *pedir que* the ending changes: *-as* becomes *-es* for an *-ar* verb.

personal: Think of something someone asked you to do today. Write it with *me pide que* or *me dice que*.
